Sign-up with verification email
Visitors create an account with email, handle and password, and the server sends a verification link to that address through Mailpit, as qualified in Business rules and Services.

Single-use expiring links
Verification and reset links work once, expire after the published lifetime measured on the server process's own clock, and stop working once a newer link of the same kind is issued, as qualified for overlapping requests in Business rules.

Verification gate
Until an account's email is verified, the friends, party, matchmaking and chat endpoints reject it with the email-unverified error from API.

Sign-in and sessions
Players sign in with email and password, receive an HTTP-only session cookie, see in the app shell who they are signed in as, with their own party row marked as theirs, and end the session by signing out.

Password reset
A player requests a reset link by email and sets a new password through it, and the request never reveals whether the email has an account.

Mail outage handling
When Mailpit is unreachable, sign-up still succeeds and reports the verification email as failed, resend and reset answer with the mail-unavailable error, and resend works again once mail is back.

Account journey
In the browser a visitor signs up, opens the emailed link, sees the verified confirmation, and lands in the app with the unverified banner gone.

Friend requests
Verified players send friend requests by handle, accept, decline or withdraw them, and remove friends, following the replay and rejection rules in API.

Crossed requests merge
Two players who send each other friend requests at the same moment end up with exactly one accepted friendship and no pending request.

Presence
Each friend shows as offline, online, in a party or in a match, derived from WebSocket heartbeats and party state, as qualified in Business rules.

Friends and presence journey
In two browsers, one player adds the other by handle, the other accepts from the rail, and each sees the other's presence dot change when they join a party and when they disconnect.

Blocking
Blocking a player removes the friendship, cancels pending friend requests and party invites both ways, and stops direct messages and presence both ways until unblocked.

Block journey
From a profile page a player blocks a friend and sees them leave the rail, and the blocked player sees the blocker vanish from theirs.

Party invites and size cap
The leader invites accepted friends into a party of at most four, and invitees join by accepting, with the rejections listed in API.

One leader with succession
Every party has exactly one leader, only the leader can queue, cancel or hand over leadership, and when the leader leaves, the member who has been in the party longest takes over.

Party journey
Four friends in four browsers form one party, all see the same grouped members and leader badge in the rail and on the stage, and all see leadership pass when the leader leaves.

Queue and cancel
The leader queues an idle party and can cancel while it is still queued, following the party state machine in Business rules.

Whole-party seating
Each queued party is seated whole in one 12-seat lobby or not at all, and concurrent placements never overfill a lobby or split a party.

Lobby countdown
A lobby starts its countdown only when every seat is filled, cancels it and reopens the seat when a seated player leaves, and starts the match when the countdown ends, as qualified in Business rules.

Lobby journey
The leader presses Find a match, the party watches the seats fill in the Lobby view, the countdown appears when the lobby is full, and everyone sees it cancel when a player leaves.

Fixed-tick 3D physics
The server simulates every round in 3D at a fixed tick rate, with gravity, jump, dive, spinning sweepers, moving platforms, bumpers and falls, on a course generated from the round's published seed, as qualified in Business rules.

Deterministic re-simulation
The same seed, starters, accepted inputs and forfeits always produce the same positions, finish order and eliminations, and these match both the frames broadcast live and the stored results.

Input acceptance and storage
The server accepts a player's input only inside the published tick window, rejects every other input with a reason, and stores the effective input for each player and tick, plus each forfeit, in PostgreSQL, as qualified in Business rules.

Qualification rules
Each round's slot count is derived once from its kind and its number of starters and stored; race and final slots fill in finish order with same-tick ties broken by ascending player id, while survival keeps its survivors under the separate selection and time-limit rules in Business rules.

Match round flow
A match runs a race, a survival round and a final, each moving through pending, running and resolved, finishes with one winner or none, and returns every party to idle with the same members.

Play controls
WASD or the arrow keys, Space and Shift, and the on-screen touch controls on narrow and touch screens produce the published input buttons, which the server stores.

Spectating after elimination
A player who is out of play keeps watching as a spectator: the Match region's data-following-user-id names the remaining player the spectator camera follows, starting with a party friend still in play, and buttons switch it.

Match journey
A party plays a full match in the browser, sees the 3D course and live standings, gets a qualified or eliminated banner, spectates, and returns to the party view together.

Party chat and direct messages
Party members chat in the party channel and friends message each other directly, with history stored in PostgreSQL, the limits in API, and unread counts on the dock tabs as qualified in Business rules.

Voice with mute and push-to-talk
In the supported voice environment, party members join peer-to-peer voice, mute themselves or switch to push-to-talk, the server relays signalling only among a party's voice members, and every member's voice tile data shows who is connected, muted and speaking.

Chat and voice journey
Two party members exchange chat messages in the dock and join voice, and each sees the other's tile change when they mute or hold the push-to-talk key.

Profiles and match history
Each player's profile counts their finished matches and wins and lists their newest finished matches with their placement, as qualified in API and Business rules, linking to each match and its rounds, and the rail links to your own profile.

Frames API
For any resolved round, the frames endpoint returns every bean's position, state and rank at a requested tick, re-simulated from the stored seed, inputs and forfeits.

Photo-finish lane list and playhead
The photo-finish view has a playhead slider and a lane list whose rows carry the same tick, position and rank as the frames endpoint, and the keyboard and dragging give identical results.

Photo-finish motion
On every playhead change, every 3D bean mesh glides to its recorded position over the published glide time as shown by data-beans, the replay camera flies to the leading bean on jumps as shown by data-camera, and the slots-left numeral updates within one frame, while reduced motion replaces each movement with a cut.

Photo-finish journey
A player opens a rival's profile, opens a past match, scrubs a round's photo-finish to its deciding tick, and sees who took the last slot.

Deployment and server boundary
The app runs from the run manifest, answers the health check, accepts same-origin requests only within the size limits, and never serves source files or credentials.

Responsive layout
The rail, stage and dock rearrange as described for viewports 375, 768 and 1280 pixels wide, with no horizontal overflow.

Keyboard and screen-reader access
Every control is reachable in a logical Tab order with a visible focus ring, dialogs keep focus inside and return it when closed, and every role and name in Public screens and controls exists.

Bean identity
Every player appears as a bean in the hue derived from their user id, and that hue is the same in the API and in every SVG bean.

Interface motion
Lobby beans bob gently, panels and banners move with the timings described, nothing else loops, and reduced motion removes each movement.

Feedback states
Every async action shows a pending state and its exact success, error or outage copy, announced in the Notices live region.

Visual design
Screens follow the cream, ink, pink, teal and red colour roles, the display and body typefaces with tabular numbers, comfortable density, and the rail-stage-dock composition, with bean hues scored under DP-40 instead.

Signature replay craft
On a still screenshot of the 3D photo-finish, the finish line, the lane order, the last-slot bean and the playhead read at a glance in the composition and match the brand's style; across screenshots before and after a playhead jump the replay camera has reframed onto the leading bean; every visible 3D bean mesh plainly carries its player's hue.

Honest wiring
Credentials come from the environment, the simulation and qualification run on the server, the match and replay are real WebGL scenes whose bean meshes, spectator camera and replay camera are driven by the server's positions and the hue rule, and voice uses real microphone capture and peer connections, as read in the source.
/app/run.json exists, with "_schema":"run-manifest-v1" and string install, build and serve commands that build and serve the app as described in Deployment.

/app/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md lists every shipped package (name, version, licence) and every shipped font (family, file, licence); a package ships when /app/package.json lists it under dependencies or optionalDependencies, along with every package those depend on in turn as installed; devDependencies hold build and test tooling only, so after the build npm prune --omit=dev leaves an app that still serves the same pages; a font ships when its file is in the app outside node_modules, build output included.
Shipped packages use only MIT, ISC, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause or Apache-2.0 licences, and shipped fonts use only OFL-1.1, with the two allowlists kept separate.

PostgreSQL is the only datastore: no other database, cache server, object storage, replay archive or file-based store, and no replay video or snapshot files; the photo-finish re-simulates from inputs stored in PostgreSQL.

At runtime the app contacts no host other than its configured services, except the direct WebRTC voice connections between party members' own browsers: fonts, icons and scripts are self-hosted, and voice uses no external STUN or TURN servers.
Server and browser source is TypeScript, compiled with strict type checking.
The provided service compose files and seeded service configuration stay unchanged.
